Start · The 45/60 plan

Read this once, slowly. It tells you which questions to pick and how to write them so the marks land even on a bad day.

How this page works

Every question in the bank is here, in the bank's order, grouped by chapter (rail at the top). Each one has up to three boxes:

ThinkThe picture or the one idea behind it. Read this while studying.
WriteExactly what goes on the answer script. In the exam hall, this is all you need.
TrapThe mistake that costs marks.

Tap Exam mode in the rail to hide every Think box and leave only the answers. Stars come from the bank: ★★ = asked almost every year, ★ = asked twice or more. Every number on this page was recomputed in Python.

What the paper looks like

The 2021-22 final (the one paper we have in full) had two groups. Each group had the same three questions:

QuestionYou answerMarksWhat they are
Shortany 5 of 85 × 2definitions, one-line checks
Mediumany 4 of 64 × 5a small calculation or a short explanation
Longany 2 of 32 × 10one big calculation (z-transform, circular convolution, DFT)

There is a choice in every question. You never have to touch the scary one. 45 out of 60 is 75 %, so the whole game is: recognise the questions you have a recipe for, pick those, and write them completely.

And the theory that is asked nearly every year, worth memorising word for word: sampling theorem, Dirichlet conditions, pole and zero, roll-off, ripple, stop-band, spectral inversion, when circular = linear, DFT and z-transform, FFT saving, overlap-add/save.

Five rules for the answer script

  1. Formula first, numbers second. Write the general formula, then substitute. If the arithmetic slips, the method marks are already on the page.
  2. Every X(z) gets "ROC: …". A z-transform without its ROC is half an answer, and this teacher cuts for it.
  3. Mark n=0. Put an arrow ↑ under the n=0 sample in every sequence you write. If the question shows no arrow, write "taking the first sample at n=0" and carry on.
  4. Sketches get labels. Name both axes, number the n ticks, write the value on top of each stem.
  5. Check one number before moving on. The checks are cheap:
    • convolution: ∑y=(∑x)(∑h), and the length is L+M−1;
    • circular convolution: ∑y=(∑x1​)(∑x2​) as well;
    • autocorrelation: symmetric, biggest at lag 0, and rxx​(0) = energy;
    • DFT: X(0)=∑x(n) and, for even N, X(N/2)=∑(−1)nx(n);
    • causal inverse z: x(0)=limz→∞​X(z).

If you only have a few hours

  • 3 hours: bankers 1–8 (about 90 min, do each once on paper), then the theory list (45 min), then Doomsday.
  • 1 hour: bankers 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, the theory list, Doomsday.
  • 15 minutes: Doomsday only. It has every formula and recipe on one screen.

1 · Continuous-time signals

Proakis ch 1, 4.1, 6.1–6.3. Mostly 2- and 5-mark theory, plus two bankers: the Nyquist rate of a sum of sinusoids and the energy by Parseval.

1.1 Signals and classification

Analog, discrete-time and digital signals

F14

“Define analog, discrete and digital signal. Show with figure.”

Write

Analog (continuous-time) signal: defined for every value of time t, and its amplitude can be any value in a continuous range. Example: the voltage from a microphone, xa​(t).

Discrete-time signal: defined only at discrete instants t=nT; the amplitude is still continuous. x(n)=xa​(nT), n an integer.

Digital signal: discrete in time and in amplitude: each sample takes one of a finite set of levels, so it can be stored as bits. (Draw the three sketches above.)

Multi-channel and multi-dimensional signals

★ F22 · TT1

“Give examples of a multi-channel and a multi-dimensional natural signal.”

ThinkMulti-channel = several signals of one variable (time). Multi-dimensional = one signal of several variables.
Write

Multi-channel: several sources or sensors recorded together, each a function of time. Examples: the 12-lead ECG; the ground acceleration of an earthquake measured in 3 directions, S(t)=[s1​(t), s2​(t), s3​(t)]T; stereo audio.

Multi-dimensional: one signal that depends on more than one independent variable. Examples: a picture I(x,y) (2-D: brightness at each point); black-and-white video I(x,y,t) (3-D).

Advantages and disadvantages of DSP over analog processing

★ TT1

Write

Advantages

  1. Flexible: change the program, not the circuit.
  2. Accurate and stable: accuracy is set by the word length; no drift with temperature, ageing or component tolerance.
  3. Storage: signals are stored on memory without loss and can be processed off-line.
  4. Powerful algorithms: adaptive filters, exact linear phase, FFT, things analog circuits cannot do.
  5. Cheap and repeatable: one processor can serve many channels; every copy behaves identically.

Disadvantages

  1. Speed / bandwidth: limited by the A/D sampling rate and processor speed, so very wide-band signals still need analog processing.
  2. Quantization error and finite word-length effects.
  3. Extra hardware: anti-aliasing filter, A/D, D/A, so more complexity and power.

The Dirichlet conditions

★ F21-22 · F24 · F21

ThinkThey answer one question: when does the Fourier series of a periodic signal really add up to that signal? Three "no wild behaviour" rules.
Write

A periodic signal x(t) with period Tp​ has a Fourier series that converges to x(t) if:

  1. x(t) has a finite number of discontinuities in any period;
  2. x(t) has a finite number of maxima and minima in any period;
  3. x(t) is absolutely integrable over a period: ∫Tp​​∣x(t)∣dt<∞.

Then the series equals x(t) wherever x(t) is continuous, and equals the midpoint 21​[x(t−)+x(t+)] at a jump. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary. (For the Fourier transform of an aperiodic signal: the same three over the whole line, ∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣dt<∞.)

1.2 Concept of frequency

Highest frequency of a CT and a DT signal; why ω=π is the top

★ F22 · TT1 · F14

ThinkA continuous cosine can wiggle as fast as you like. A sampled one can only change at integer n; the fastest it can do is flip sign at every sample, (−1)n, which is cos(πn).
Write

CT: xa​(t)=Acos(2πFt) is distinct for every F, so −∞<F<∞: there is no highest frequency.

DT: frequencies are unique only in −π≤ω≤π (that is −21​≤f≤21​). The highest is ∣ω∣=π, which corresponds to F=Fs​/2.

Proof that the top is at ω=π: take x(n)=cosω0​n. For ω0​=0,8π​,4π​,2π​,π the period is ∞,16,8,4,2, so it oscillates faster as ω0​ grows. At ω0​=π, x(n)=cosπn=(−1)n, which changes sign at every sample: nothing can be faster. For π<ω0​<2π write ω0​=2π−ω1​ with 0<ω1​<π:

cosω0​n=cos(2πn−ω1​n)=cosω1​n

so it is the same as the slower ω1​. The rate of oscillation rises up to ω=π and falls after it, so the highest frequency is at ω=±π.

Frequency range and sampling rate of human speech

★ F22 · TT1

WriteSpeech has almost all its energy between about 100 Hz and 4 kHz (the telephone channel passes 300–3400 Hz). So telephone speech is sampled at Fs​=8 kHz =2×4 kHz, i.e. 8000 samples per second. (Wide-band speech: 16 kHz; music CDs: 44.1 kHz for a 20 kHz band.)

1.3 Sampling theorem and Nyquist

State the sampling theorem; Nyquist rate and Nyquist interval

★★ F17 · F24 · F21-22 · F22

ThinkSample faster than twice the fastest wiggle and the samples pin the curve down: the spectrum copies made by sampling do not overlap, so a low-pass filter gives back the original.
Write

Sampling theorem. If the highest frequency in an analog signal xa​(t) is Fmax​=B (the signal is band-limited), then xa​(t) can be recovered exactly from its samples x(n)=xa​(nT) provided the sampling rate satisfies

Fs​>2Fmax​=2B

The recovery uses the ideal interpolation formula

xa​(t)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)g(t−nT),g(t)=πt/Tsin(πt/T)​

Nyquist rate FN​=2Fmax​: the minimum sampling rate that avoids aliasing.
Nyquist interval TN​=2Fmax​1​: the largest sampling interval allowed.
Folding frequency Fs​/2: the highest frequency that sampling at Fs​ represents uniquely.

Nyquist rate of a sum of sinusoids, and the sampled x(n)

★★ F24 · DSPTT1 · TT1 · NEW

“Find the Nyquist rate for x(t)=30cos50πt+10sin300πt−2cos100πt, and determine x[n] after sampling at Fs​=5000 samples/s.”

ThinkIn cos(50πt) the number in front of πt is 2F, so halve it: 50πt means 25 Hz. Nyquist rate = twice the biggest F. To sample, replace t by n/Fs​.
Write

F1​=2π50π​=25 Hz, F2​=2π300π​=150 Hz, F3​=2π100π​=50 Hz. So Fmax​=150 Hz and

Nyquist rate=2Fmax​=300 Hz

Sampling at Fs​=5000 Hz (>300, no aliasing), put t=n/5000:

x(n)=30cos100πn​+10sin503πn​−2cos50πn​
Same recipe, other papers
  • x(t)=3sin1500πt+10sin4260πt−cos250πt: F=750, 2130, 125 Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 4260 Hz. TT1
  • ECG with frequencies up to 100 Hz: Nyquist rate 200 Hz. Sampled at 250 samples/s, the highest frequency represented uniquely is Fs​/2= 125 Hz. TT1

xa​(t)=sin480πt+3sin720πt sampled 600 times a second

★ F21 · TT1

“(i) Nyquist rate (ii) folding frequency (iii) x(n) (iv) frequencies in rad (v) the reconstructed ya​(t) from an ideal D/A.”

Think600 is below the Nyquist rate (720), so the 360 Hz tone aliases to 600−360=240 Hz and lands on top of the other tone.
Write

(i) F1​=240 Hz, F2​=360 Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 2×360=720 Hz.

(ii) Folding frequency =Fs​/2=300 Hz.

(iii) Put t=n/600:

x(n)=sin(0.8πn)+3sin(1.2πn)

1.2π>π, so subtract 2π: sin(1.2πn)=sin(1.2πn−2πn)=sin(−0.8πn)=−sin(0.8πn). Hence

x(n)=sin(0.8πn)−3sin(0.8πn)=−2sin(0.8πn)

(iv) ω1​=2π⋅600240​=0.8π rad/sample; ω2​=2π⋅600360​=1.2π rad/sample, which is outside (−π,π] and appears as −0.8π.

(v) The ideal D/A rebuilds only frequencies below 300 Hz, putting n=600t:

ya​(t)=−2sin(480πt)=xa​(t)

The difference is aliasing, because Fs​=600<720.

1.4 Aliasing

What is aliasing? Show it graphically (time and frequency)

★★ F24 · F17 · F21-22 · TT1

ThinkTwo different analog frequencies that differ by a multiple of Fs​ give exactly the same samples. After sampling you cannot tell them apart, so the high one pretends to be ("takes the alias of") the low one.
Write

Aliasing: when xa​(t) is sampled at Fs​<2Fmax​, a frequency F0​>Fs​/2 gives the same samples as the lower frequency F0​−kFs​ that lies in [−Fs​/2, Fs​/2]. The reconstructed signal then contains the wrong (alias) frequency.

Example: x1​(t)=cos2π(10)t and x2​(t)=cos2π(50)t sampled at Fs​=40 Hz:

x1​(n)=cos2π​n,x2​(n)=cos25π​n=cos(2πn+2π​n)=cos2π​n

Identical: 50 Hz is an alias of 10 Hz at this rate.

Time domain:

Frequency domain: sampling repeats the analog spectrum every Fs​:

X(F)=Fs​k=−∞∑∞​Xa​(F−kFs​)

If Fs​≥2Fmax​ the copies stay apart and a low-pass filter of width Fs​/2 returns Xa​(F). If Fs​<2Fmax​ the copies overlap (red), the high frequencies fold back below Fs​/2, and xa​(t) cannot be recovered.

1.5 A/D, quantization, D/A

These have long, drawn answers in your other file, 30-ch1-adc-dac-answers.html. Below is the short version of each.

A/D block diagram, the ideal sample-and-hold, and X(F) when Fs​<2Fmax​

F17

Write

A/D converter: xa​(t)→ Sampler →x(n)=xa​(nT)→ Quantizer →xq​(n)→ Coder → bits. The sampler makes time discrete, the quantizer makes amplitude discrete (rounds to the nearest level), the coder writes each level as a b-bit word.

Ideal sample-and-hold: a switch and a capacitor. In sample mode the output follows xa​(t); at t=nT it switches to hold and keeps xa​(nT) constant while the A/D converts it. Ideal = instant switching, no droop, no timing jitter, so the held value is exactly xa​(nT).

Spectrum: X(F)=Fs​∑k​Xa​(F−kFs​), copies of Xa​(F) every Fs​. If Fs​<2Fmax​ the copies overlap: aliasing, and xa​(t) cannot be recovered (see 1.4).

Quantization of a sinusoid (midtread) and how to reduce the error

★ F14 · F17 · TT1

Write

Each sample is rounded to the nearest of the allowed levels, which are Δ apart. In a midtread quantizer, 0 is one of the levels (the staircase has a flat step at 0). The quantization error eq​(n)=xq​(n)−x(n) always lies in

−2Δ​≤eq​(n)≤2Δ​

To reduce it: make Δ smaller by using more levels, that is more bits b (Δ=range/(L−1), L=2b). Each extra bit halves Δ and adds about 6 dB of SQNR. Also: round instead of truncating, and use the full range of the quantizer.

x(n)=6.35cos(πn/10) with Δ=0.1 (and 0.02): how many bits?

★ F21 · TT1

Write

Range =xmax​−xmin​=6.35−(−6.35)=12.7. Number of levels L=Δrange​+1.

  • Δ=0.1: L=127+1=128=27, so 7 bits.
  • Δ=0.02: L=635+1=636; 29=512<636≤1024=210, so 10 bits.
TrapDon't forget the "+1" (levels at both ends), and round the bits up.

Digital to analog conversion; SQNR and how to change it

★ F22 · TT1 · NEW

Write

D/A: bits → decoder (each word becomes a voltage level) → sample-and-hold / zero-order hold (keeps each value for T seconds, giving a staircase) → analog low-pass (smoothing) filter with cut-off Fs​/2, which removes the sharp steps (the high-frequency images) and leaves a smooth ya​(t). (Draw the D/A row of the figure above.)

SQNR (signal-to-quantization-noise ratio) =Pq​Px​​, the signal power over the quantization-noise power, with Pq​=12Δ2​. For a full-scale sinusoid and b bits:

SQNR=1.76+6.02b dB

Each extra bit adds about 6 dB. SQNR is reduced by using fewer bits (larger Δ); in practice we want it high, so we use more bits, use the full range of the quantizer, or use non-uniform quantization (companding).

1.6 The sketch questions

4 Hz sampled at 10 Hz; 10 Hz at 20 Hz; a 3 Hz sine

★ F22 · TT1 · IMG(TT1)

ThinkThe digital frequency is f=F/Fs​. It tells you the pattern: f=2/5 repeats every 5 samples, f=1/2 is the ±1 flip.
Write

4 Hz at 10 Hz F22: xa​(t)=sin(2π⋅4t), one period is 0.25 s, T=0.1 s. x(n)=sin(2π⋅104​n)=sin(0.8πn), f=2/5, so the samples repeat every N=5 (covering 2 analog cycles). One analog period holds 2.5 samples. Values for n=0..4: 0, 0.588, −0.951, 0.951, −0.588. Then quantize, define SQNR as above.

10 Hz at 20 Hz TT1: exactly 2 samples per period. With a cosine, x(n)=cosπn=(−1)n={1,−1,1,−1,…}; with a sine every sample is sinπn=0 and the signal vanishes. That is why the theorem needs Fs​>2Fmax​ strictly.

3 Hz sine IMG(TT1): period 1/3 s. The sampling rate is the number of samples per second, Fs​=1/T; here it must exceed 6 Hz. At Fs​=12 Hz, x(n)=sin(πn/2)={0,1,0,−1,…}. System function: H(z)=Y(z)/X(z) (see 2.1). Reduce quantization error: more bits.

1.7 Frequency analysis of CT signals

Fourier series vs Fourier transform

★ F17 · F14 · TT2

ThinkSeries: a periodic signal is a sum of harmonics, so its spectrum is lines. Transform: a one-off signal needs every frequency, so its spectrum is a continuous curve. Let the period grow to infinity and the lines merge into the curve.
Write
Fourier seriesFourier transform
Forperiodic signals (power signals)aperiodic signals (finite energy)
Synthesisx(t)=∑k​ck​ej2πkF0​tx(t)=∫X(F)ej2πFtdF
Analysisck​=Tp​1​∫Tp​​x(t)e−j2πkF0​tdtX(F)=∫x(t)e−j2πFtdt
Spectrumdiscrete lines at kF0​continuous in F
Parsevalpower =∑∣ck​∣2energy =∫∣X(F)∣2dF

The transform is the limit of the series as Tp​→∞: the line spacing F0​=1/Tp​→0 and Tp​ck​→X(F).

Power density spectrum of a periodic signal; the rectangular pulse train

★★ F17 · F22 · ★ F21

Write

Definition. For a periodic x(t) with Fourier coefficients ck​, Parseval's relation gives the average power

Px​=Tp​1​∫Tp​​∣x(t)∣2dt=k=−∞∑∞​∣ck​∣2

The plot of ∣ck​∣2 against F=kF0​ shows how the power is shared among the harmonics: this is the power density spectrum. It is a set of lines spaced F0​=1/Tp​ apart, and for a real signal it is even (∣c−k​∣=∣ck​∣).

Rectangular pulse train (height A, width τ, period Tp​, centred at 0):

c0​=Tp​1​∫−τ/2τ/2​Adt=Tp​Aτ​ ck​=Tp​1​∫−τ/2τ/2​Ae−j2πkF0​tdt=Tp​Aτ​πkF0​τsin(πkF0​τ)​,k=0 ∣ck​∣2=(Tp​Aτ​)2(πkF0​τsinπkF0​τ​)2

Lines at F=k/Tp​ under a sinc2 envelope whose zeros are at F=±1/τ,±2/τ,… Total power =A2τ/Tp​.

Energy of xa​(t)=e−αt, t≥0, α=0.6, by Parseval

★★ F22 · F21-22

ThinkParseval says energy is the same counted in time or in frequency. Find X(F), square its size, integrate. The time-domain integral is a one-line check.
Write X(F)=∫0∞​e−αte−j2πFtdt=α+j2πF1​,∣X(F)∣2=α2+(2πF)21​

By Parseval's theorem, E=∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣2dt=∫−∞∞​∣X(F)∣2dF. Put u=2πF, dF=du/2π:

E=2π1​∫−∞∞​α2+u2du​=2π1​⋅απ​=2α1​

With α=0.6: E=1.21​=0.833 J.

Check in time: ∫0∞​e−2αtdt=2α1​=0.833. ✓

Trap∫α2+u2du​=α1​tan−1αu​, which runs from −2π​ to 2π​: total απ​.

1.8 Modulation

Modulation and demodulation

F24

Write

Modulation: varying a parameter (amplitude, frequency or phase) of a high-frequency carrier in step with the message signal, to move the message to a frequency band suited to the channel (small antennas, many signals sharing a medium by FDM). Amplitude modulation: y(t)=A[1+mx(t)]cos2πFc​t.

Demodulation: the reverse, at the receiver: recovering the original message x(t) from the modulated carrier (e.g. multiply by the carrier again and low-pass filter, or an envelope detector for AM).

Proakis 2.1, 1.3.2. Cheap, reliable marks: periodicity, energy/power and the sketches are pure recipes.

2.1 Elementary signals and representation

Write a sequence with u(n) and with δ(n)

★ F22 · TT2 · F17 · F21

“Express x(n)={1,1,1,1,1} in terms of u(n) and of δ(n).” · “Resolve x(n)={2,4,0,3} into a sum of weighted impulses.”

Thinkδ(n−k) is a single 1 sitting at n=k. u(n)−u(n−N) is a block of N ones starting at 0 (switch on at 0, switch off at N). Any sequence is "each sample times an impulse at its position".
Write

Taking the first sample at n=0, x(n)={↑1​,1,1,1,1} for 0≤n≤4:

x(n)=u(n)−u(n−5) x(n)=δ(n)+δ(n−1)+δ(n−2)+δ(n−3)+δ(n−4)=k=0∑4​δ(n−k)

(If the arrow is under the middle 1, so −2≤n≤2: x(n)=u(n+2)−u(n−3)=∑k=−22​δ(n−k).)

Any x(n) in terms of δ(n) F17:

x(n)=k=−∞∑∞​x(k)δ(n−k)

x(n)={2,↑4​,0,3} (Proakis's version, arrow under 4) F21: x(−1)=2, x(0)=4, x(1)=0, x(2)=3, so

x(n)=2δ(n+1)+4δ(n)+3δ(n−2)

(If your paper has the arrow under the 2: x(n)=2δ(n)+4δ(n−1)+3δ(n−3).)

Even and odd parts; is sin(πt/7), −7≤t≤7, even or odd?

F21-22 · F24 · TT2 · NEW

ThinkEven = mirror image about n=0 (like cos). Odd = mirror image with a sign flip (like sin). Every signal splits into one of each.
Write

Even: x(−n)=x(n), e.g. cosω0​n. Odd: x(−n)=−x(n), e.g. sinω0​n. The same definitions apply to periodic signals.

Any x(n) is the sum of an even and an odd part:

xe​(n)=21​[x(n)+x(−n)],xo​(n)=21​[x(n)−x(−n)],x(n)=xe​(n)+xo​(n)

Check: xe​(−n)=21​[x(−n)+x(n)]=xe​(n) and xo​(−n)=21​[x(−n)−x(n)]=−xo​(n).

x(t)=sin(πt/7) on −7≤t≤7 (the 2021-22 paper writes sin(πt/T) on −T≤t≤T): the interval is symmetric about 0 and

x(−t)=sin(−7πt​)=−sin7πt​=−x(t)

so the signal is odd (its even part is zero). By inspection: a sine is antisymmetric about t=0.

Short ones: functional form, non-integer n, signal vs system, system function

F24 · F21 · IMG(TT1)

Write

Functional representation of x(n)={…,0,0,1,1,↑4​,1,1,0,0,…} (taking the 4 at n=0):

x(n)=⎩⎨⎧​4,1,0,​n=0n=±1,±2otherwise​

x(n) at a non-integer n: it is not defined. A discrete-time signal exists only at integer n; it is not zero in between, it simply has no value there.

DT signal vs DT system: a signal is a function of the integer n, a sequence of numbers, e.g. x(n)=(0.5)nu(n). A system is a device or algorithm that operates on an input signal to produce an output signal, y(n)=T[x(n)], e.g. y(n)=21​[x(n)+x(n−1)].

System function: the z-transform of the impulse response, equal to the ratio of the output and input z-transforms of an LTI system:

H(z)=n∑​h(n)z−n=X(z)Y(z)​=1+∑k=1N​ak​z−k∑k=0M​bk​z−k​

2.2 Periodicity of DT sinusoids

Is it periodic? What is the fundamental period?

★★ F22 · F21 · F24 · TT1 · F21-22

ThinkA DT sinusoid repeats only if a whole number of samples fits a whole number of cycles. Divide ω0​ by 2π: if you get a fraction of integers k/N, it repeats every N. If π survives in the fraction (like 3/2π), it never repeats.
Write

Condition: x(n)=cos(ω0​n+θ) is periodic with period N only if cos(ω0​(n+N)+θ)=cos(ω0​n+θ), i.e. ω0​N=2πk, i.e.

f0​=2πω0​​=Nk​is a rational number.

Reduce k/N to lowest terms; the denominator N is the fundamental period.

Signalf0​=ω0​/2πPeriodic?N
cos0.01πn0.005=1/200yes200
sin3n3/2π, irrationalno–
cos0.1πn1/20yes20

Is x(2n) causal? Is x(−n) causal?

F22 · F21

Write

A signal is causal if x(n)=0 for n<0. Take x(n) causal.

x(2n): yes. For n<0, 2n<0, so x(2n)=0. (But the system y(n)=x(2n) is non-causal: y(1)=x(2) needs a future input.)

x(−n): no. It is non-zero for n≤0, i.e. anti-causal (unless x(n) is only cδ(n)). The system y(n)=x(−n) is also non-causal: y(−1)=x(1).

2.5 Zero padding

Purpose of zero padding

F24

WriteZero padding = appending zeros to a sequence before taking an N-point DFT. It is used to:
  1. get more DFT points, i.e. a denser sampling of the spectrum X(ω), so the plotted spectrum looks smoother (it does not add real resolution: no new information);
  2. make N≥L+M−1 so that circular convolution equals linear convolution (filtering with the DFT);
  3. make the length a power of 2 for the radix-2 FFT.

3.1 Classifying a system

The five tests, each in one line

★ F22 · TT2 · F17 · F24 · TT1 · F21-22 · CSE425-TT1

ThinkLook only at the right-hand side. Where does x get evaluated (at n? n+1? 2n?), what multiplies it (a constant? n?), and is it squared or added to a constant?
Write
  • Static (memoryless) if y(n) needs x only at the same n. Anything like x(n−1), x(n+1), x(2n), x(−n) makes it dynamic.
  • Linear if T[ax1​+bx2​]=aT[x1​]+bT[x2​]. Quick signs of non-linearity: x2, ∣x∣, an added constant (zero input must give zero output). Multiplying by n or u(n) is still linear.
  • Time-invariant if delaying the input by k just delays the output by k: compare y(n,k)=T[x(n−k)] with y(n−k). A factor that depends on n (nx(n), x(n)u(n)) or a scaled/folded time (x(2n), x(−n), x(n2)) makes it time-variant.
  • Causal if y(n) uses only present and past inputs. Test one value: x(n+1); x(2n) at n=1 needs x(2); x(−n) at n=−1 needs x(1); x(n2) at n=2 needs x(4): all non-causal.
  • Stable (BIBO) if every bounded input gives a bounded output. A factor that grows with n (like nx(n)) makes it unstable.

3.2 Convolution and impulse response

Convolution: the steps, and the fast way to compute it

★★ F24 · DSPTT1 · F14 · CSE425-TT1 · IMG(TT1)

ThinkConvolution is long multiplication without carrying. Write x on top, h under it, multiply row by row shifting one place each time, add the columns. The flip-and-slide picture is the same thing drawn sideways; draw it when the question says "graphically".
Write y(n)=x(n)∗h(n)=k=−∞∑∞​x(k)h(n−k)

Steps (for each output time n):

  1. Folding: fold h(k) about k=0 to get h(−k).
  2. Shifting: shift h(−k) by n to get h(n−k) (to the right if n>0).
  3. Multiplication: multiply x(k) by h(n−k) for every k.
  4. Summation: add all the products to get y(n).

Length of y = L+M−1; first index = (first index of x) + (first index of h).

Commutative? True. Put m=n−k: ∑k​x(k)h(n−k)=∑m​h(m)x(n−m), so x∗h=h∗x. IMG(TT1)

3.4 Correlation

Define autocorrelation and cross-correlation

F14 · NEW

Write

Cross-correlation of x(n) and y(n) measures how alike x is to y shifted by l samples:

rxy​(l)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)y(n−l),l=0,±1,±2,…

Autocorrelation is a signal correlated with itself:

rxx​(l)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)x(n−l)

Properties: rxx​(−l)=rxx​(l) (even), the largest value is at l=0, and rxx​(0)=Ex​ (the energy). ryx​(l)=rxy​(−l). Correlation is convolution with one signal reversed: rxy​(l)=x(l)∗y(−l).

Example: radar. x = transmitted pulse, y = received echo; ryx​(l) peaks at the lag equal to the echo's delay, which gives the distance.

3.5 Digital filters and filter design

Roll-off, stop-band attenuation and ripple; narrow vs wide transition band

★★ F24 · TT2 · F21-22 · F17 · F14 · F22 · TT02

ThinkAn ideal low-pass is a brick wall: 1 in the pass-band, 0 in the stop-band, a vertical drop between. A real one wobbles in the pass-band (ripple), leaks a little in the stop-band (finite attenuation), and takes some width to fall (roll-off). These three numbers grade a filter.
Write

Roll-off: how sharply the response falls from the pass-band to the stop-band. It is measured by the width of the transition band: a fast roll-off means a narrow transition band, so frequencies close together can be separated.

Pass-band ripple: the wiggle of the gain inside the pass-band. It changes the amplitudes of the frequencies that should pass unchanged, so it should be as small as possible (ideally flat).

Stop-band attenuation: how strongly the stop-band frequencies are suppressed, in dB (e.g. −60 dB). Larger attenuation = better rejection of unwanted signals.

These three (with the cut-off frequency) are the frequency-domain parameters used to judge a low-pass filter.

Narrow transition band — advantages: sharp separation of nearby frequencies, close to ideal. Disadvantages: needs a long filter kernel (length M≈4/BW), so more computation, more delay, more ringing in the time domain.
Wide transition band — advantages: short kernel, fast and cheap, little ringing. Disadvantages: poor selectivity; frequencies near the cut-off are only partly removed.

Spectral inversion: high-pass from low-pass; band-pass by spectral reversal

★★ F24 · F17 · F21 · F14 · F22 · TT02

ThinkA delta passes everything (all-pass). All-pass minus low-pass leaves exactly the high frequencies. In the kernel, "minus low-pass" means flip every sign, and "plus delta" means add 1 at the centre.
Write

Spectral inversion: from a symmetric (linear-phase) low-pass kernel hLP​[n], 0≤n≤M:

  1. change the sign of every sample;
  2. add 1 to the sample at the centre of symmetry, n=M/2.
hHP​[n]=δ[n−M/2]−hLP​[n],HHP​(f)=1−HLP​(f)

The input goes through the all-pass (delta) and the low-pass in parallel and the low-pass output is subtracted, leaving only the high frequencies. The response is turned upside down; the cut-off stays where it was. (The kernel must be symmetric so the low frequencies cancel exactly.)

Spectral reversal (the other way to get a high-pass): multiply every other sample by −1, hHP​[n]=(−1)nhLP​[n]. This shifts the response by π, flipping it left-to-right: a cut-off fc​ becomes 0.5−fc​.

Band-pass from low-pass (pass fL​ to fH​): (1) design a low-pass with cut-off fH​; (2) design a low-pass with cut-off 0.5−fL​ and spectrally reverse it into a high-pass with cut-off fL​; (3) cascade them, i.e. convolve the kernels: hBP​=hLP​∗hHP​. (Alternatively: add a low-pass at fL​ and a high-pass at fH​ to get a band-reject filter, then spectrally invert it into a band-pass.)

FIR vs IIR, popular filters, filter kernel, why digital

★ F24 · F14 · F22 · F17 · TT02

Write
FIRIIR
Impulse responsefinite lengthinfinite length
Structurenon-recursive, no feedback: y(n)=∑k​bk​x(n−k)recursive, feedback: y(n)=−∑k​ak​y(n−k)+∑k​bk​x(n−k)
Stabilityalways stable (poles only at z=0)can be unstable; poles must be inside ∣z∣=1
Phaseexactly linear phase possiblenon-linear phase
Costmany coefficients for a sharp filterfew coefficients, efficient
Examplesmoving average, windowed-sincsingle-pole, Chebyshev, Butterworth

Two popular FIR filters: the moving-average filter and the windowed-sinc filter.

Two time-domain and two frequency-domain filters: time domain (smoothing, DC removal): moving average (FIR) and single-pole recursive (IIR). Frequency domain (separating bands): windowed-sinc (FIR) and Chebyshev (IIR).

Purpose of a digital filter: (1) signal separation, when a signal is mixed with noise or other signals (e.g. removing mains hum from an ECG); (2) signal restoration, when a signal has been distorted (e.g. deblurring). Filter kernel: the impulse response h[n] of a filter that is implemented by convolution, y=x∗h.

Main advantage of digital filters: far better performance than analog ones: very sharp roll-off, large stop-band attenuation, tiny pass-band ripple, exact linear phase, no drift with temperature or component tolerance, and they can be changed in software.

Designing by placing poles and zeros; what poles and zeros mean

F17 · F21-22

ThinkWalk round the unit circle: the point ejω is frequency ω. Being near a pole makes ∣H∣ big, being near a zero makes it small. So put poles where you want gain and zeros where you want silence.
Write ∣H(ω)∣=∣b0​∣∏k​∣ejω−pk​∣∏k​∣ejω−zk​∣​

Principles: a pole close to the unit circle at angle ω0​ makes the response large near ω0​; a zero on or near the circle at ω0​ makes it small (zero) there. Poles must be inside the unit circle for stability; complex poles and zeros come in conjugate pairs so the coefficients are real.

Low-pass: pole near z=1 (ω=0), zero at z=−1 (ω=π): H(z)=21−a​⋅1−az−11+z−1​. High-pass: mirror image, pole near z=−1, zero at z=1: H(z)=21−a​⋅1+az−11−z−1​ (0<a<1).

Significance: poles decide the natural behaviour: each pole p adds a term pn to h(n), decaying if ∣p∣<1, growing if ∣p∣>1, slowly if it is near the circle, oscillating if it is complex. A causal system is stable only if all poles are inside the unit circle. Poles make peaks in ∣H∣; zeros make dips or nulls. The pole-zero plot plus a gain describes the system completely.

Windowed-sinc steps; FIR low-pass by the window method

F17 · F14 · TT2

ThinkThe ideal low-pass has a sinc impulse response that goes on forever both ways. Chop it to M+1 samples, shift it to start at 0, and taper the ends with a window so the chop doesn't cause big ripples.
Write

Windowed-sinc filter, steps:

  1. Choose the cut-off fc​ (fraction of the sampling rate, 0 to 0.5) and the transition bandwidth BW; the length is M≈4/BW (even).
  2. Compute the shifted sinc: h[i]=i−M/2sin(2πfc​(i−M/2))​ for i=0..M, with h[M/2]=2πfc​.
  3. Multiply by a window, e.g. Blackman w[i]=0.42−0.5cosM2πi​+0.08cosM4πi​ (or Hamming).
  4. Normalise so that ∑h[i]=1 (unity gain at DC).
  5. Filter by convolving the signal with h. (For a high-pass, spectrally invert it.)

Window method (Proakis): desired Hd​(ω)=e−jωα for ∣ω∣≤ωc​, 0 otherwise, with α=(M−1)/2. Then

hd​(n)=2π1​∫−ωc​ωc​​ejω(n−α)dω=π(n−α)sinωc​(n−α)​,h(n)=hd​(n)w(n), 0≤n≤M−1

Rectangular window: narrowest main lobe but high side lobes (−13 dB), so large ripple (Gibbs). Hanning (−31 dB), Hamming (−41 dB), Blackman (−57 dB): less ripple but a wider transition band. A larger M narrows the transition band.

Why an ideal filter cannot be built

TT2 · F21-22

Write

The ideal low-pass filter, H(ω)=1 for ∣ω∣≤ωc​ and 0 otherwise, has the impulse response

h(n)=πnsinωc​n​,−∞<n<∞
  1. h(n)=0 for n<0: the filter is non-causal, it would need future inputs;
  2. h(n) is infinitely long, so it needs infinite memory and computation;
  3. ∑∣h(n)∣=∞, so it is not even BIBO stable.

(Paley–Wiener: a causal filter cannot have ∣H∣=0 over a whole band or a vertical edge.) So real filters truncate and window h(n) and accept ripple and a transition band.

Is the median filter time-invariant? Is h(n)=anu(n) stable?

F21-22 · ★ F22 · TT3

Write

Median filter y(n)=med{x(n−k),…,x(n),…,x(n+k)}. Delay the input, x1​(n)=x(n−n0​):

y1​(n)=med{x(n−n0​−k),…,x(n−n0​+k)}=y(n−n0​)

so it is time-invariant. (It is non-linear: for windows {3,0,0} and {0,0,3} the medians are 0 and 0, but the median of the sum {3,0,3} is 3.)

Stability condition: an LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if its impulse response is absolutely summable, ∑n​∣h(n)∣<∞ (equivalently, for a causal system, all poles inside the unit circle).

h(n)=anu(n), ∣a∣<1:n=0∑∞​∣a∣n=1−∣a∣1​<∞

so it is stable.

Magnitude and phase of the 3-point and 5-point moving-average filters

★ F24 · F21-22

ThinkPull out the middle delay, e−jω(M−1)/2, and the rest pairs up into cosines, so it is real. The real part is the magnitude (up to sign) and the pulled-out factor is the phase: a straight line, which flips by π wherever the real part changes sign.
Write

General M-point: h(n)=1/M for 0≤n≤M−1,

H(ejω)=M1​n=0∑M−1​e−jωn=M1​1−e−jω1−e−jωM​=M1​sin(ω/2)sin(Mω/2)​e−j(M−1)ω/2

H(ejω)=31​(1+e−jω+e−j2ω)=31​e−jω(ejω+1+e−jω)=31​(1+2cosω)e−jω ∣H(ejω)∣=31​∣1+2cosω∣,θ(ω)={−ω,−ω+π,​∣ω∣<2π/32π/3<ω≤π​

∣H∣=1 at ω=0, 0 at ω=2π/3, 31​ at ω=π.

H(ejω)=51​e−j2ω(ej2ω+ejω+1+e−jω+e−j2ω)=51​(1+2cosω+2cos2ω)e−j2ω ∣H(ejω)∣=51​∣1+2cosω+2cos2ω∣,θ(ω)=−2ω (+π for 2π/5<ω<4π/5)

Zeros at ω=±2π/5,±4π/5; ∣H∣=1 at 0 and 51​ at π. Both are low-pass filters with linear phase.

Causal FIR h[n]={−3,6,−5,4}, input Acosω0​n: frequency response

F21-22

Write H(ejω)=n=0∑3​h(n)e−jωn=−3+6e−jω−5e−j2ω+4e−j3ω

Real and imaginary parts: HR​=−3+6cosω−5cos2ω+4cos3ω, HI​=−6sinω+5sin2ω−4sin3ω, so ∣H∣=HR2​+HI2​​ and θ(ω)=tan−1(HI​/HR​).

A sinusoid comes out as the same sinusoid, scaled and shifted:

4.1 Circular convolution

Circular convolution of x1​(n)=[1,1,2,1] and x2​(n)=[1,2,3,4], illustrated

★★ F24

ThinkSame as ordinary convolution, but the sequences live on a clock with N positions: anything that slides off the end comes back at the start. The matrix does the wrapping for you: each row is the previous row rotated one place to the right.
Write y(m)=x1​(n)⊛x2​(n)=n=0∑N−1​x1​(n)x2​((m−n))N​,m=0,1,…,N−1

Matrix method. First row: x2​(0) followed by the rest of x2​ backwards, [x2​(0),x2​(3),x2​(2),x2​(1)]; every next row is the previous one rotated right by one.

​y(0)y(1)y(2)y(3)​​=​1234​4123​3412​2341​​​1121​​=​1+4+6+22+1+8+33+2+2+44+3+4+1​​=​13141112​​ y(n)={↑13​,14,11,12}

Graphical (concentric circles): write x1​(n) counter-clockwise on the outer circle and x2​(−n) (i.e. x2​ clockwise) on the inner circle, both starting at the same point. Multiply facing pairs and add: that is y(0). Turn the inner circle one step counter-clockwise for y(1), and so on.

Check: ∑y=50=(∑x1​)(∑x2​)=5×10. ✓

The other versions, and when circular = linear

F21-22 · TT02 · NEW · ★ F22 · F24 · F21-22

Write

[1,1,2,1]⊛[1,2,1,1] F21-22:

When does circular convolution equal linear convolution? If x1​ has length L and x2​ has length M, the linear result has length L+M−1. Pad both with zeros to length N; the N-point circular convolution equals the linear one when

N≥L+M−1

If N is smaller, the tail of the linear result wraps round and adds onto the first samples (time-domain aliasing): ycirc​(n)=∑l​ylin​(n+lN).

4.2 DFT definition and derivation

Derive the DFT pair from the Fourier transform of an aperiodic DT signal

★ F24 · F17

ThinkThe DTFT X(ω) is a continuous curve; a computer can only keep N points of it. Sample it at ωk​=2πk/N. Sampling in frequency makes the time signal periodic, and if x(n) is no longer than N the copies don't overlap, so nothing is lost.
Write

The Fourier transform of an aperiodic sequence is X(ω)=∑n=−∞∞​x(n)e−jωn, periodic in ω with period 2π. Sample it at N equally spaced frequencies ωk​=2πk/N:

X(N2πk​)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)e−j2πkn/N=l=−∞∑∞​ n=lN∑lN+N−1​x(n)e−j2πkn/N

Put n→n−lN in the inner sum and use e−j2πk(n−lN)/N=e−j2πkn/N:

X(N2πk​)=n=0∑N−1​[xp​(n)l∑​x(n−lN)​​]e−j2πkn/N,k=0,…,N−1

xp​(n) is the periodic extension of x(n) (period N), so it has a Fourier series xp​(n)=∑k=0N−1​ck​ej2πkn/N with ck​=N1​∑n=0N−1​xp​(n)e−j2πkn/N=N1​X(2πk/N). Hence

xp​(n)=N1​k=0∑N−1​X(N2πk​)ej2πkn/N

If x(n) has finite length L≤N, the copies in xp​(n) do not overlap and x(n)=xp​(n) for 0≤n≤N−1. Writing X(k)=X(2πk/N) gives the DFT pair:

X(k)=n=0∑N−1​x(n)e−j2πkn/N,x(n)=N1​k=0∑N−1​X(k)ej2πkn/N

How is the DFT related to the Fourier transform and to the z-transform? Why is it so important?

★ F24 · F21-22 · F17 · F14 · TT02

ThinkThree views of the same thing. z-transform: the whole complex plane. Fourier transform: its values on the unit circle. DFT: N evenly spaced dots on that circle.
Write

DFT and Fourier transform: the DFT is the Fourier transform X(ω) sampled at N equally spaced frequencies:

X(k)=X(ω)​ω=2πk/N​,k=0,1,…,N−1

DFT and z-transform: for x(n) of length L≤N, X(z)=∑n=0N−1​x(n)z−n; putting z=ej2πk/N gives the DFT:

X(k)=X(z)​z=ej2πk/N​,k=0,1,…,N−1

So the DFT is the z-transform evaluated at N equally spaced points on the unit circle. (Conversely X(z)=N1−z−N​k=0∑N−1​1−ej2πk/Nz−1X(k)​.)

Why the DFT matters: it is the only Fourier transform a computer can actually compute, because it is finite and discrete in both time and frequency; the FFT computes it fast (Nlog2​N); and it is used for spectrum analysis, fast linear filtering (overlap-add/save), correlation and convolution.

(magnitude 1, phase linear in k.)

4.3 DFT properties

Phase factor WN​: symmetry, W4100​=Wx200​, periodicity of X(k), linearity

F22 · F21 · F21-22 · NEW · F24 (zero padding: 2.5)

Write

WN​=e−j2π/N, a point on the unit circle; its powers walk round the circle in N steps.

  • Symmetry: WNk+N/2​=−WNk​, because WNN/2​=e−jπ=−1.
  • Periodicity: WNk+N​=WNk​, because WNN​=e−j2π=1.
  • Also WN2​=WN/2​ (used by the FFT).

If W4100​=Wx200​, find x: e−j2π⋅100/4=e−j2π⋅200/x, so 4100​=x200​, giving x=8. (In general WNk​=W2N2k​; both sides equal e−j50π=1.)

X(k) is periodic with period N:

X(k+N)=n=0∑N−1​x(n)e−j2π(k+N)n/N=n=0∑N−1​x(n)e−j2πkn/N=1e−j2πn​​=X(k)

Linearity: if x1​↔X1​(k) and x2​↔X2​(k) (both N-point), then

DFT{ax1​(n)+bx2​(n)}=n=0∑N−1​[ax1​(n)+bx2​(n)]WNkn​=aX1​(k)+bX2​(k)

(If the lengths differ, zero-pad both to N≥max(N1​,N2​).)

Write X(ejω)=n=0∑∞​ane−jωn=n=0∑∞​(ae−jω)n=1−ae−jω1​,∣a∣<1

(The series converges because ∣ae−jω∣=∣a∣<1.) For real a: ∣X∣=1−2acosω+a2​1​, θ=−tan−11−acosωasinω​.

4.5 Windowing and filtering with the DFT

How the choice of window affects frequency analysis; short-time spectrum

★ F22 · F21 · F14 · TT02

ThinkYou can only take the DFT of a finite piece, which is the signal multiplied by a window. Multiplying in time smears in frequency: every sharp spectral line gets replaced by the window's own spectrum, a main lobe (blur) with side lobes (leakage).
Write

Analysing L samples means using x^(n)=x(n)w(n). Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency:

X^(ω)=2π1​∫−ππ​X(θ)W(ω−θ)dθ

e.g. for x(n)=cosω0​n with a rectangular window, X^(ω)=21​[W(ω−ω0​)+W(ω+ω0​)]: a spread-out sinc instead of a single line. Two effects:

  1. Resolution is limited by the main-lobe width (about 4π/L for rectangular): two frequencies closer than that merge.
  2. Leakage comes from the side lobes: power spills into other frequencies and can hide weak components.

Choice: rectangular has the narrowest main lobe (best resolution) but the highest side lobes (−13 dB, most leakage). Hanning, Hamming and Blackman have lower side lobes (less leakage) but wider main lobes (poorer resolution). A longer window improves both. For a short-time spectrum the window length is a trade-off: short = good time detail but poor frequency resolution; long = the opposite.

Linear convolution of {1,2,1} and {2,3,4} via DFT/IDFT; Y(k)=X1​(k)X2​(k) for [0,1,2,3], [0,1,0,0]

CSE425-TT2 · F14

ThinkThe DFT turns convolution into multiplication, but only circular convolution. Pad to N≥L+M−1 and circular becomes linear. Neat trick: with W=WNk​, a DFT is just a polynomial in W, so multiplying DFTs is multiplying polynomials, which is convolution.
Write

L=M=3, so N≥3+3−1=5. Pad both to N=5 (or 8 for a radix-2 FFT), take DFTs, multiply, take the IDFT:

X(k)=1+2W+W2,H(k)=2+3W+4W2,W=W5k​ Y(k)=X(k)H(k)=2+7W+12W2+11W3+4W4

No power of W reaches 5, so nothing wraps, and the IDFT reads off the coefficients:

y(n)={↑2​,7,12,11,4}

Check: Y(0)=X(0)H(0)=4×9=36=∑y. ✓

x1​=[0,1,2,3], x2​=[0,1,0,0], Y(k)=X1​(k)X2​(k): a product of DFTs is a 4-point circular convolution. Here x2​=δ(n−1), so X2​(k)=W4k​ and y(n)=x1​((n−1))4​, a circular shift by one:

y(n)={↑3​,0,1,2}
Numbers, if they insist5-point DFTs: X(k)={4, 0.809−j2.490, −0.309−j0.224, −0.309+j0.224, 0.809+j2.490}; H(k)={9, −0.309−j5.204, 0.809+j2.041, 0.809−j2.041, −0.309+j5.204}; Y(k)={36, −13.208−j3.441, 0.208−j0.812, 0.208+j0.812, −13.208+j3.441}.

Filtering long data: overlap-add and overlap-save

★ F22 · F21 · F17 · F14 · TT02 · CSE425-TT2

ThinkThe input is too long for one DFT, so cut it into blocks and filter each with the DFT. The only problem is the edges: each block's output is M−1 samples longer than the block. Overlap-add lets those tails overlap and adds them; overlap-save makes the input blocks overlap instead and throws away the M−1 corrupted outputs.
Write

Filter h(n) has length M; input blocks have L new samples; DFT size N=L+M−1. Pad h(n) with L−1 zeros and compute H(k) once.

Overlap-add:

  1. Cut x(n) into non-overlapping blocks of L samples.
  2. Append M−1 zeros to each block (length N), take its N-point DFT, multiply by H(k), take the IDFT. Each output block is the full linear convolution, N long.
  3. Consecutive output blocks overlap by M−1 samples: add the overlapping parts.

Overlap-save:

  1. Each input block has N samples: the last M−1 samples of the previous block followed by L new ones (the first block starts with M−1 zeros).
  2. Take its N-point DFT, multiply by H(k), take the IDFT (a circular convolution).
  3. The first M−1 outputs of each block are corrupted by wrap-around: discard them and keep the last L. Join the kept pieces.

This is how long sequences are filtered without direct convolution: block-by-block with the FFT, much faster than direct convolution.

5 · FFT: decimation in time and frequency

DFT vs FFT, the condition on N, the basic idea, the properties used

★ F17 · F21 · F14 · NEW

Write

DFT vs FFT: the DFT is the transform itself (the definition X(k)=∑x(n)WNkn​). The FFT is not a different transform: it is a family of fast algorithms that compute exactly the same X(k) with far fewer operations (2N​log2​N instead of N2 multiplications).

Condition: the radix-2 FFT needs N=2v, a power of 2 (zero-pad otherwise). In general the FFT needs N to be a composite number, N=r1​r2​⋯rv​.

Basic idea (divide and conquer): split the N-point DFT into two N/2-point DFTs (even and odd samples), split those again, and so on down to 2-point DFTs; reuse the shared products at each level.

Properties of WN​ it uses:

  • symmetry: WNk+N/2​=−WNk​
  • periodicity: WNk+N​=WNk​
  • WN2​=WN/2​

Derive the decimation-in-time FFT; describe the radix-2 algorithm

★ F22 · F17 · F21

Write

Let N=2v. Split x(n) into even and odd samples: f1​(m)=x(2m), f2​(m)=x(2m+1), m=0,…,N/2−1.

X(k)=m=0∑N/2−1​x(2m)WN2mk​+m=0∑N/2−1​x(2m+1)WN(2m+1)k​

Since WN2​=WN/2​:

X(k)=m=0∑N/2−1​f1​(m)WN/2km​+WNk​m=0∑N/2−1​f2​(m)WN/2km​=F1​(k)+WNk​F2​(k)

F1​ and F2​ are N/2-point DFTs, so they repeat with period N/2; and WNk+N/2​=−WNk​. Therefore, for k=0,1,…,N/2−1:

X(k)=F1​(k)+WNk​F2​(k)​ X(k+N/2)=F1​(k)−WNk​F2​(k)​

This pair is the butterfly: one complex multiplication, two additions. Apply the same split to F1​ and F2​, and repeat until only 2-point DFTs remain.

Radix-2 algorithm: v=log2​N stages, each with N/2 butterflies, so 2N​log2​N multiplications. In DIT the input is in bit-reversed order and the output in natural order; the computation is in place. (DIF splits the output instead: X(2k)=∑n=0N/2−1​[x(n)+x(n+N/2)]WN/2kn​ and X(2k+1)=∑n=0N/2−1​[x(n)−x(n+N/2)]WNn​WN/2kn​; natural input, bit-reversed output.)

4-point DIT butterfly flow graph

Write

Stage 1: F1​(0)=x(0)+x(2), F1​(1)=x(0)−x(2), F2​(0)=x(1)+x(3), F2​(1)=x(1)−x(3).

Stage 2: X(0)=F1​(0)+F2​(0), X(2)=F1​(0)−F2​(0), X(1)=F1​(1)−jF2​(1), X(3)=F1​(1)+jF2​(1).

Divide and conquer: steps, illustrated for N=15

F14

ThinkFold the 15 samples into a 5×3 table. Do small DFTs along the rows, fix up with twiddle factors, do small DFTs down the columns, read the answer off row by row.
Write

Write N=LM=5×3 (L=5 rows, M=3 columns).

  1. Store the signal column-wise: x(l,m)=x(l+mL), so row l holds x(l),x(l+5),x(l+10).
  2. Compute the M-point (3-point) DFT of each row: F(l,q)=∑m=02​x(l,m)W3mq​, q=0,1,2.
  3. Multiply by the phase factors: G(l,q)=W15lq​F(l,q).
  4. Compute the L-point (5-point) DFT of each column: X(p,q)=∑l=04​G(l,q)W5lp​, p=0,…,4.
  5. Read the result row-wise: X(k) with k=Mp+q=3p+q.
m=0m=1m=2
l=0x(0)x(5)x(10)
l=1x(1)x(6)x(11)
l=2x(2)x(7)x(12)
l=3x(3)x(8)x(13)
l=4x(4)x(9)x(14)

Cost: N(M+L+1)=15×9=135 complex multiplications instead of N2=225. (Checked in Python against a direct FFT.)

6 · The z-transform

Proakis ch 3. Two of the three 10-markers usually come from here. The whole chapter rests on one pair, anu(n)↔1−az−11​, and one habit: write the ROC every time.

6.1 Definition, ROC, poles and zeros

Definition, ROC, pole and zero

★★ F22 · F24 · F21 · F21-22 · F14 · ★ F17 · TT3

ThinkX(z) is a power series in z−1; it only adds up to something finite for some z. That set is the ROC, and it is always bounded by circles through the poles (the ROC never contains a pole).
Write X(z)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)z−n

ROC (region of convergence): the set of all z for which this sum converges, i.e. X(z) is finite.

Zero: a value of z where X(z)=0 (a root of the numerator). Pole: a value of z where X(z)=∞ (a root of the denominator). Pole-zero plot: poles marked × and zeros marked ○ in the z-plane, with the unit circle dashed. Example: X(z)=z−az​ has a zero at z=0 and a pole at z=a.

SequenceROC
finite, causal (only z−k)all z except z=0
finite, anti-causal (only zk)all z except z=∞
finite, two-sidedall z except 0 and ∞
δ(n)the entire z-plane
infinite, causal∣z∣>r: outside the outermost pole
infinite, anti-causal∣z∣<r: inside the innermost pole
infinite, two-sideda ring r1​<∣z∣<r2​ (or nothing)

Finite-duration anti-causal example: x(n)={1,2,↑3​} gives X(z)=z2+2z+3, ROC: all z except z=∞.

ThinkDo the two halves separately. The right-sided half converges outside ∣a∣, the left-sided half inside ∣b∣. Both must hold at once, so the ROC is the ring between, and if there is no ring there is no z-transform.
Write X(z)=n=0∑∞​anz−n+n=−∞∑−1​bnz−n

First sum: 1−az−11​, converges for ∣z∣>∣a∣.

Second sum, with m=−n: ∑m=1∞​(b−1z)m=1−b−1zb−1z​=−1−bz−11​, converges for ∣z∣<∣b∣.

X(z)=1−az−11​−1−bz−11​=(1−az−1)(1−bz−1)(a−b)z−1​ ROC: ∣a∣<∣z∣<∣b∣

If ∣b∣>∣a∣ the ROC is a ring (sketch: shade the annulus between the circles of radius ∣a∣ and ∣b∣, poles × at a and b, as in the right panel of the ROC figure). If ∣b∣≤∣a∣ there is no common region and X(z) does not exist.

6.3 Inverse z-transform

The recipe: partial fractions, then let the ROC choose each term

used by every question below

ThinkEvery pole p gives a term pn. The ROC decides which way it runs: if the ROC is outside the pole, the term runs right (causal, u(n)); if inside, it runs left (anti-causal, −u(−n−1)).
Write
  1. Write X(z) in powers of z−1. If the numerator's degree is not lower than the denominator's, divide first.
  2. Factor the denominator: (1−p1​z−1)(1−p2​z−1).
  3. Partial fractions: X(z)=1−p1​z−1A1​​+1−p2​z−1A2​​. Cover-up: A1​ = the rest of X(z) with z−1=1/p1​ put in.
  4. Invert each term using the ROC:

ROC outside the pole (∣z∣>∣p∣), causal:

1−pz−1A​⟷Apnu(n)

ROC inside the pole (∣z∣<∣p∣), anti-causal:

1−pz−1A​⟷−Apnu(−n−1)

Also: (1−z−1)21​↔(n+1)u(n), (1−az−1)2az−1​↔nanu(n), z−kX(z)↔x(n−k). Stable means the ROC contains the unit circle.

Fourier transform vs z-transform; the shifting property; z-transform of a convolution

★ F24 · F21 · F17

Write

Relation: put z=rejω:

X(z)​z=rejω​=n∑​[x(n)r−n]e−jωn

so the z-transform is the Fourier transform of x(n)r−n. On the unit circle (r=1) it is the Fourier transform itself:

X(ω)=X(z)​z=ejω​

valid only if the ROC contains the unit circle (e.g. u(n), ROC ∣z∣>1, has no ordinary Fourier transform).

Shifting property: x(n−k)↔z−kX(z), same ROC except possibly z=0 (for k>0) or z=∞ (for k<0). Proof: ∑n​x(n−k)z−n=∑m​x(m)z−(m+k)=z−kX(z). (For convolution: if y=x∗h, then x(n−k)∗h(n)=y(n−k).)

Convolution:

x1​(n)∗x2​(n)⟷X1​(z)X2​(z),ROC⊇ROC1​∩ROC2​

Proof: ∑n​∑k​x1​(k)x2​(n−k)z−n=∑k​x1​(k)z−k∑m​x2​(m)z−m with m=n−k.

Last · Doomsday sheet

Fifteen minutes before the exam. If you remember only this, you can still write every banker.

Signals (ch 1–2)

  • cos(Kπt) has F=K/2 Hz. Nyquist rate =2Fmax​; interval =1/(2Fmax​); folding =Fs​/2. Sample: t→n/Fs​.
  • Alias: F0​>Fs​/2 looks like F0​−kFs​. ω above π: subtract 2π.
  • Bits: L=range/Δ+1, b=⌈log2​L⌉. SQNR =1.76+6.02b dB; error ∈[−Δ/2,Δ/2].
  • Periodic iff ω0​/2π=k/N rational; N = reduced denominator. Sum: LCM.
  • E=∑∣x∣2; P=lim2N+11​∑−NN​∣x∣2. (−1)n: E=∞, P=1. u(n): E=∞, P=21​.
  • Sketch x(an+b): sample at m moves to n=(m−b)/a; drop non-integers.
  • xe​=21​[x(n)+x(−n)], xo​=21​[x(n)−x(−n)]. x(n)=∑k​x(k)δ(n−k).
  • Parseval: e−αtu(t) has E=1/2α (0.833 for α=0.6). Pulse train: ck​=Tp​Aτ​πkF0​τsinπkF0​τ​, PSD =∣ck​∣2.

Systems (ch 3)

  • Static: only x(n). Linear: no x2, no constant. TI: no n outside x(⋅), no x(2n), x(−n). Causal: no argument above n. Stable: no growing factor.
  • Convolution = long multiplication without carry; start = sum of starts; length L+M−1; check ∑y=∑x∑h.
  • Correlation rxy​(l)=x(l)∗y(−l): reverse y, multiply. Autocorrelation symmetric, peak r(0) = energy.
  • y=ay(n−1)+bx(n)⇒h=banu(n). Cascade: convolve; parallel: add.
  • M-point MA: H=M1​sin(ω/2)sin(Mω/2)​e−j(M−1)ω/2. 3-pt: 31​(1+2cosω)e−jω.
  • Stable LTI: ∑∣h∣<∞ (poles inside unit circle).
  • Filter grades: roll-off (transition band), pass-band ripple, stop-band attenuation. Narrow transition = sharp but long kernel.
  • Spectral inversion: negate all, +1 at centre (δ−hLP​). Reversal: (−1)nh, flips fc​→0.5−fc​.
  • FIR: finite, no feedback, always stable, linear phase. IIR: feedback, can be unstable, fewer coefficients.

DFT and FFT (ch 4–5)

  • X(k)=∑n=0N−1​x(n)WNkn​, x(n)=N1​∑X(k)WN−kn​, WN​=e−j2π/N. N=4: powers 1,−j,−1,j.
  • DFT = DTFT at ω=2πk/N = z-transform at z=ej2πk/N.
  • Circular conv: matrix, first row [x2​(0),x2​(3),x2​(2),x2​(1)], rotate right each row. Equals linear if N≥L+M−1.
  • WNk+N/2​=−WNk​, WNk+N​=WNk​, WN2​=WN/2​. W4100​=W8200​.
  • FFT: 2N​log2​N vs N2 mult. DIT: X(k)=F1​(k)+WNk​F2​(k), X(k+2N​)=F1​(k)−WNk​F2​(k); bit-reversed input 0,2,1,3 / 0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7.
  • Overlap-add: blocks of L, pad M−1 zeros, add the tails. Overlap-save: blocks of N overlapping M−1, drop the first M−1 outputs.
  • Window: main lobe = resolution, side lobes = leakage. Rectangular: sharpest, leakiest.

z-transform (ch 6)

  • anu(n)↔1−az−11​, ∣z∣>∣a∣. −anu(−n−1)↔ same, ∣z∣<∣a∣.
  • nanu(n)↔(1−az−1)2az−1​ (from −zdX/dz). (1−z−1)21​↔(n+1)u(n). δ(n−k)↔z−k.
  • Finite an, 0..M−1: 1−az−11−aMz−M​, M−1 zeros at aej2πk/M, M−1 poles at 0.
  • Two-sided anu(n)+bnu(−n−1): 1−az−11​−1−bz−11​, ROC ∣a∣<∣z∣<∣b∣ (else none).
  • Inverse: factor, cover-up, then ROC outside pole →pnu(n); inside →−pnu(−n−1). Stable ⇔ ROC holds ∣z∣=1.
  • X(ω)=X(z)∣z=ejω​ if the ROC contains the unit circle. x(−n)↔X(z−1).
  • Write the ROC under every X(z).
